Describing a robot

Ch 2

Configuration space

A robot’s configuration specifies the configuration of all its links. The dimension of its C-space is the number of degrees of freedom.

\[\class{sym-dof}{\text{dof}}=\class{sym-grm}{m}\,(\class{sym-grN}{N}-1-\class{sym-grJ}{J})+\sum_{i=1}^{\class{sym-grJ}{J}}\class{sym-grf}{ f_i}\]

In words: Degrees of freedom = freedoms of the moving links minus the constraints the joints impose.

  • dof degrees of freedom
  • m freedoms of one rigid body
  • N number of links, ground included
  • J number of joints
  • fi freedoms of joint i
Key terms
ConfigurationConfiguration spaceDegrees of freedomGrübler's formulaHolonomic constraintTask space
Ch 2 · Eq. 2.4Open topic →
Ch 3

Rigid-body motions

Rotations R ∈ SO(3) and rigid-body motions T ∈ SE(3) describe frames. Velocities are twists 𝒱 along screw axes; moments and forces form wrenches ℱ.

\[\class{sym-V}{\mathcal V}=\class{sym-S}{\mathcal S}\,\class{sym-th3dot}{\dot\theta}\]

In words: A twist is a screw axis times the rate of motion about it.

  • 𝒱 twist (angular, linear velocity)
  • 𝒮 screw axis
  • θ̇ rate of rotation about the axis
Key terms
Rotation matrixHomogeneous transformationScrew axisTwistWrenchAdjoint map
Ch 3 · §3.3.2Open topic →
Ch 4

Forward kinematics

Forward kinematics maps the joint values θ to the configuration T(θ) of the end-effector frame {b} in {s}, using only M and the screw axes.

\[\class{sym-Tee}{T}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})=\class{sym-expm}{e}^{\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-Si}{\mathcal S_1}\class{sym-brk}{]}\class{sym-theta}{\theta_1}}\cdots\class{sym-expm}{ e}^{\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-Si}{\mathcal S_n}\class{sym-brk}{]}\class{sym-theta}{\theta_n}}\class{sym-M}{M}\]

In words: Each joint’s screw motion, applied to the home configuration M, gives the end-effector configuration.

  • T(θ) end-effector configuration
  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
  • e[·] matrix exponential
  • 𝒮i screw axis of joint i, in {s}
  • [·] bracket: skew-symmetric or se(3) matrix
  • M end-effector configuration at home
Key terms
Forward kinematicsProduct of exponentials (PoE)Zero positionDenavit–Hartenberg parametersURDF
Ch 4 · Eq. 4.14Open topic →

Velocities and inverses

Ch 5

Jacobian and statics

The Jacobian J(θ) relates the joint rates θ̇ to the end-effector twist 𝒱. Its transpose maps an end-effector wrench ℱ to joint torques τ.

\[\class{sym-Vs}{\mathcal V_s}=\class{sym-Js}{J_s}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})\,\class{sym-thetad}{\dot\theta}\]

In words: The space Jacobian maps joint velocities to the end-effector’s spatial twist.

  • 𝒱s spatial twist (in {s})
  • Js space Jacobian
  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
  • θ̇ joint velocities
Key terms
JacobianSpace JacobianBody JacobianKinematic singularityManipulability ellipsoidStatics of open chains
Ch 5 · Eq. 5.10Open topic →
Ch 6

Inverse kinematics

Inverse kinematics finds joint values θ with T(θ) = X. There may be several solutions or none; numerical methods iterate from an initial guess.

\[\class{sym-theta}{\theta}^{i+1}=\class{sym-theta}{\theta}^{i}+\class{sym-Jbdag}{J_b^{\dagger}}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta}^{i})\,\class{sym-Vb}{\mathcal V_b}\]

In words: Each iteration steps the joints by the body Jacobian’s pseudoinverse times the body twist to the goal.

  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
  • Jb† pseudoinverse of the body Jacobian
  • 𝒱b body twist (in {b})
Key terms
Inverse kinematicsAnalytic inverse kinematicsNumerical inverse kinematicsNewton–Raphson methodPseudoinverseKinematic redundancy
Ch 6 · §6.2.2Open topic →
Ch 7

Closed chains

A closed chain contains one or more loops. Only some joints are actuated, and the joint variables must satisfy loop-closure constraint equations.

\[\class{sym-di}{d_i}=\class{sym-p7}{p}+\class{sym-bi}{b_i}-\class{sym-ai}{a_i}\]

In words: Each leg vector closes a loop: platform position plus platform point minus base point.

  • di vector along leg i
  • p platform position in {s}
  • bi leg i attachment on the platform
  • ai leg i attachment on the base
Key terms
Closed chainParallel mechanismStewart–Gough platformAssembly modeActuator singularity
Ch 7 · Eq. 7.1Open topic →

Dynamics and motion

Ch 8

Dynamics

The equations of motion τ = M(θ)θ̈ + c(θ, θ̇) + g(θ) follow from the Euler–Lagrange equations or from the recursive Newton–Euler algorithm.

\[\class{sym-tau}{\tau}=\class{sym-Mth}{M}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})\class{sym-thetadd}{\ddot\theta}+\class{sym-c}{c}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta},\class{sym-thetad}{\dot\theta})+\class{sym-g}{g}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})\]

In words: Joint torques = mass matrix × acceleration + Coriolis and centripetal terms + gravity terms.

  • τ joint torques and forces
  • M(θ) mass matrix
  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
  • θ̈ joint accelerations
  • c(θ, θ̇) Coriolis and centripetal terms
  • θ̇ joint velocities
  • g(θ) gravity terms
Key terms
Mass matrixEuler–Lagrange equationsNewton–Euler inverse dynamicsForward dynamicsInverse dynamicsGear ratio
Ch 8 · Eq. 8.10Open topic →
Ch 9

Trajectory generation

A trajectory θ(s(t)) combines a path θ(s) with a time scaling s(t): cubic, quintic, trapezoidal, S-curve, or time-optimal under actuator limits.

\[\class{sym-theta}{\theta}(\class{sym-t}{t})=\class{sym-theta}{\theta}\big(\class{sym-s}{s}(\class{sym-t}{t})\big),\qquad\class{sym-s}{ s}:[0,\class{sym-Tmot}{T}]\to[0,1]\]

In words: A trajectory is a path θ(s) timed by a time scaling s(t) that runs from 0 to 1.

  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
  • t time
  • s path parameter, 0 to 1
  • T total motion time
Key terms
PathTime scalingTrajectoryQuintic time scalingTrapezoidal motion profileTime-optimal time scaling
Ch 9 · §9.1Open topic →
Ch 10

Motion planning

Motion planning finds a collision-free motion from start to goal. Obstacles split C-space into Cfree and Cobs; planners search graphs, grids or random samples.

\[\class{sym-C}{\mathcal C}=\class{sym-Cfree}{\mathcal C_{\text{free}}}\cup\class{sym-Cobs}{\mathcal C_{\text{obs}}}\]

In words: The C-space splits into free configurations and configurations in collision.

  • 𝒞 configuration space (C-space)
  • 𝒞free free space
  • 𝒞obs C-obstacle space
Key terms
C-obstacleFree spaceA* searchRRTPRMVirtual potential field
Ch 10 · §10.2.1Open topic →

Control and the world

Ch 11

Robot control

Feedback control drives the error θe to zero. The error response is judged by overshoot, 2% settling time and steady-state error.

\[\class{sym-tau}{\tau}=\class{sym-Kp}{K_p}\class{sym-the}{\theta_e}+\class{sym-Ki}{K_i}\!\int\class{sym-the}{\theta_e}(\class{sym-t}{t})\,dt+\class{sym-Kd}{K_d}\class{sym-thedot}{\dot\theta_e}\]

In words: Torque proportional to the joint error, its integral and its derivative.

  • τ joint torques and forces
  • Kp proportional gain
  • θe joint error θd − θ
  • Ki integral gain
  • t time
  • Kd derivative gain
  • θ̇e rate of joint error
Key terms
Error dynamicsPID controlComputed torque controlForce controlHybrid motion–force controlImpedance control
Ch 11 · Eq. 11.23Open topic →
Ch 12

Grasping and manipulation

Contact kinematics, a friction model and rigid-body dynamics solve contact problems. Contacts are labeled R, S or B; closure decides whether a grasp holds.

\[\class{sym-Fc}{\mathcal F}^{\mathsf T}(\class{sym-VA}{\mathcal V_A}-\class{sym-VB}{\mathcal V_B})\ge 0\]

In words: Two bodies in contact may separate or slide but never move into each other.

  • ℱ contact wrench
  • 𝒱A twist of body A
  • 𝒱B twist of body B
Key terms
Contact normalFriction coneForm closureForce closureWrench cone
Ch 12 · Eq. 12.5Open topic →
Ch 13

Wheeled mobile robots

Chassis configuration: q = (φ, x, y). A nonholonomic robot obeys A(q)q̇ = 0; an omnidirectional robot, with omniwheels or mecanum wheels, does not.

\[\class{sym-A13}{A}(\class{sym-q13}{q})\,\class{sym-q13d}{\dot q}=\begin{bmatrix}0&\sin\class{sym-phi13}{\phi}&-\cos\class{sym-phi13}{\phi}\end{bmatrix}\class{sym-q13d}{\dot q}=0\]

In words: The no-slip constraint: the chassis cannot move sideways.

  • A(q) Pfaffian constraint matrix
  • q chassis configuration (φ, x, y)
  • q̇ chassis velocity
  • φ chassis heading angle
Key terms
Chassis configurationNonholonomic mobile robotOmnidirectional robotDifferential driveOdometry

Part 1 · Ch 2 · Configuration space

02How many numbers does it take to say where a robot is?

A configuration specifies the position of every point of a robot. Count the numbers it takes, and find the shape of the space they fill.

Ch 2 · §2.1–2.52 playgroundsQuiz · 3 questions

Orientation

Why this exists

Before a robot can reach for a cup, we need a way to write down where it is. Its pose is a list of numbers, such as joint angles. How many numbers, and the shape of the space they live in, decide how many motors it needs and how planners search.

After this you can
  • Count the dof of a rigid body, open chain or mechanism with Grübler's formula.
  • Describe the shape (topology) of a C-space, such as a torus or a sphere.
  • Choose between an explicit and an implicit representation of a C-space.
  • Tell holonomic constraints from nonholonomic (Pfaffian) velocity constraints.
  • Distinguish the configuration space, the task space and the workspace.
How it connects
← Builds onBasicsVectors, angles, equationsCh 1Robots as links and joints
Leads to →Ch 3Rigid-body motionsCh 7Closed chainsCh 10Motion planningCh 13Wheeled mobile robots

Key concepts

Configuration

A specification of the position of every point of the robot.

See it in the lab ↗

Degrees of freedom (dof)

The smallest number of real-valued coordinates needed to represent the configuration.

See it in the lab ↗

Configuration space (C-space)

The set of all configurations of the robot. Its dimension equals the dof.

See it in the lab ↗

Joint

A connection between two links that allows some relative motion and constrains the rest.

See it in the lab ↗

Topology

The shape of a space, which stays the same under stretching but not cutting or gluing.

See it in the lab ↗

Holonomic constraint

A constraint on configurations of the form g(θ) = 0 that reduces the dimension of the C-space.

See it in the lab ↗

Nonholonomic constraint

A Pfaffian velocity constraint A(θ)θ̇ = 0 that cannot be integrated into a configuration constraint.

See it in the lab ↗

Task space

The space in which the robot's task is naturally expressed, such as the end-effector's position and orientation.

See it in the lab ↗

Worked example

Degrees of freedom of the Stewart–Gough platform

Ch 2 · §2.2
Ex. 2.8§2.2.2Simplified: side view
Grübler's formula Eq. 2.4
dof = m(N − 1 − J) + Σfi
m = 6 · N = 14 · J = 18 · Σfi = 36
= 6(14 − 1 − 18) + 36 = −30 + 36 = 6
= 6(14 − 1 − 18) + 42 = 12 with S for U

In words: Grübler’s formula for the Stewart–Gough platform: 14 links and 18 joints leave 6 degrees of freedom.

  • dof degrees of freedom
  • m freedoms of one rigid body
  • N number of links, ground included
  • J number of joints
  • Σ sum over the J joints
  • fi freedoms of joint i

Given. The Stewart–Gough platform: a fixed base and a moving platform joined by six UPS legs. The bodies move in space, so m = 6.

Count the links. Ground, the platform, and two parts per leg, a cylinder and a rod: N = 1 + 1 + 12 = 14.

Count the joints. Each leg has a universal, a prismatic and a spherical joint: J = 6 × 3 = 18.

Sum the freedoms. U gives 2, P gives 1 and S gives 3, so Σfᵢ = 6(2) + 6(1) + 6(3) = 36.

Result. dof = 6(14 − 1 − 18) + 36 = 6. The platform moves with all six freedoms of a rigid body.

Variant. With spherical joints at both ends, Σfᵢ = 42 and dof = 12. The six extra freedoms are leg spins that leave the platform still.

The rule

Grübler's formula: m = 3 planar, 6 spatial; N links incl. ground; J joints §2.2
\[\class{sym-dof}{\text{dof}} =\class{sym-grm}{ m}\,(\class{sym-grN}{N}-1-\class{sym-grJ}{J}) + \sum_{i=1}^{\class{sym-grJ}{J}}\class{sym-grf}{ f_i}\]
(2.4)

In words: Degrees of freedom = freedoms of all the moving links minus the independent constraints the joints impose.

  • dof degrees of freedom
  • m freedoms of one rigid body
  • N number of links, ground included
  • J number of joints
  • fi freedoms of joint i
Pfaffian velocity constraint §2.4
\[\class{sym-A}{A}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})\,\class{sym-thetad}{\dot{\theta}} = 0\]

In words: Loop-closure constraints, differentiated in time, allow only the joint velocities that keep the loops closed.

  • A(θ) Pfaffian constraint matrix
  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
  • θ̇ joint velocities
Spherical surface: explicit vs implicit §2.3
\[(\class{sym-lat}{\text{lat}},\class{sym-lon}{\text{lon}}) \quad\text{vs}\quad\class{sym-x3}{ x}^2+\class{sym-y3}{y}^2+\class{sym-z3}{z}^2 = 1\]

In words: Two numbers (latitude, longitude) name a point on the sphere explicitly; three coordinates with one constraint name it implicitly.

  • lat latitude
  • lon longitude
  • x first Cartesian coordinate
  • y second Cartesian coordinate
  • z third Cartesian coordinate

Part 1 · Ch 3 · Rigid-body motions

03Rotations, transforms, twists and wrenches

Attach a frame to a body and describe the frame. Rotations, transforms, twists and wrenches all follow from one idea: the screw motion.

Ch 3 · §3.1–3.42 playgroundsQuiz · 3 questions

Orientation

Why this exists

A robot that picks up a part must know where the part and its gripper are, and how to move one onto the other. Rotation matrices, transforms, twists and wrenches describe position, orientation, motion and force for any rigid body. Every later chapter speaks this language.

After this you can
  • Use R ∈ SO(3) and T ∈ SE(3) to represent, change and move frames.
  • Tell a rotation about a fixed-frame axis (premultiply) from one about a body-frame axis (postmultiply).
  • Go between a rotation and its exponential coordinates ω̂θ with the matrix exponential and logarithm.
  • Write any rigid motion as a screw axis 𝒮 and distance θ: T = e[𝒮]θ.
  • Express twists and wrenches in any frame with the adjoint map, and compute power 𝒱ᵀℱ.
How it connects
← Builds onCh 2Configuration spaceBasicsVectors, angles, equations
Leads to →Ch 4Forward kinematicsCh 5Jacobian and staticsCh 8DynamicsCh 12Grasping

Key concepts

SO(3)

The special orthogonal group: all 3×3 real matrices R with RᵀR = I and det R = 1.

See it in the lab ↗

SE(3)

The special Euclidean group: 4×4 matrices T built from R ∈ SO(3) and p ∈ ℝ³.

See it in the lab ↗

Space and body frames

{s} is a fixed frame. {b} is a frame attached to the moving body.

See it in the lab ↗

Skew-symmetric matrix [ω]

The 3×3 matrix with [ω]x = ω × x. The set of these is so(3).

See it in the lab ↗

Exponential coordinates

ω̂θ ∈ ℝ³ for a rotation, or 𝒮θ ∈ ℝ⁶ for a rigid motion: an axis times a distance.

See it in the lab ↗

Screw axis 𝒮

A normalized twist (ω, v), with either ‖ω‖ = 1, or ω = 0 and ‖v‖ = 1.

See it in the lab ↗

Twist 𝒱

A spatial velocity (ω, v) that combines angular and linear velocity, 𝒱 = 𝒮θ̇.

See it in the lab ↗

Wrench ℱ

A spatial force (m, f) that combines a moment and a linear force.

See it in the lab ↗

Where it happens

Worked example

The screw that moves one frame onto another

Ch 3 · §3.3.3
Ex. 3.26§3.3.3.2
Screw motion from {b} to {c} §3.3.3.2
TscTsb−1 = e[𝒮]θ
𝒮 = (0, 0, 1, 3.37, −3.37, 0), θ = 0.524 rad
ω × q = −v → q = (3.37, 3.37), h = 0

In words: The displacement from {b} to {c} is one screw motion: a 30° turn about the vertical axis through q = (3.37, 3.37).

  • Tsc configuration of {c} in {s}
  • Tsb configuration of {b} in {s}
  • e[·] matrix exponential
  • 𝒮 screw axis
  • θ angle turned about the axis
  • ω rotation axis (angular part of 𝒮)
  • q a point on the screw axis
  • v linear part of 𝒮
  • h screw pitch

Given. Two frames in the plane: {b} at (1, 2) turned 30°, and {c} at (2, 1) turned 60°. Find the screw motion that takes {b} to {c}.

Displacement in {s}. TscTsb−1 is a 30° rotation with translation (2.13, −1.23). It must equal e[𝒮]θ.

Matrix logarithm. The log gives ω = (0, 0, 1), θ = 0.524 rad (30°) and v = (3.37, −3.37, 0).

Find the axis. The pitch is zero, so v = −ω × q. Solving gives the axis point q = (3.37, 3.37), 2.73 from both origins.

Result. Rotating {b} by 30° about q lands exactly on {c}: Tsc = e[𝒮]θTsb.

The rule

Rodrigues' formula §3.2.3
\[\class{sym-Rot}{\text{Rot}}(\class{sym-omegahat}{\hat\omega},\class{sym-th3}{\theta})=\class{sym-expm}{e}^{\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-omegahat}{\hat\omega}\class{sym-brk}{]}\class{sym-th3}{\theta}}=\class{sym-Ieye}{I}+\sin\class{sym-th3}{\theta}\,\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-omegahat}{\hat\omega}\class{sym-brk}{]}+(1-\cos\class{sym-th3}{\theta})\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-omegahat}{\hat\omega}\class{sym-brk}{]}^2\]
(3.51)

In words: Rotating by the angle θ about the unit axis ω̂ gives this rotation matrix, computed in closed form from [ω̂].

  • Rot(ω̂, θ) rotation by θ about ω̂
  • ω̂ unit rotation axis
  • θ angle (or distance) along the axis
  • e[·] matrix exponential
  • [·] bracket: skew-symmetric or se(3) matrix
  • I identity matrix
Homogeneous transform §3.3
\[\class{sym-T}{T}=\begin{bmatrix}\class{sym-R}{R} &\class{sym-p}{ p}\\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\in\class{sym-SE3}{ SE(3)},\qquad\class{sym-T}{ T} =\class{sym-expm}{ e}^{\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-S}{\mathcal S}\class{sym-brk}{]}\class{sym-th3}{\theta}}\]

In words: A configuration stacks a rotation R and a position p into one 4×4 matrix; every such T is a screw motion.

  • T homogeneous transformation matrix
  • R rotation matrix
  • p position of the frame origin
  • SE(3) special Euclidean group
  • e[·] matrix exponential
  • 𝒮 screw axis
  • [·] bracket: skew-symmetric or se(3) matrix
  • θ angle (or distance) along the axis
Changing frames, and power §3.3.2, §3.4
\[\class{sym-Va}{\mathcal V_a}=[\class{sym-Ad}{\mathrm{Ad}}_{\class{sym-T-ab}{T_{ab}}}]\,\class{sym-Vb}{\mathcal V_b},\qquad\class{sym-Pow}{ P}=\class{sym-V}{\mathcal V}^{\mathsf T}\class{sym-F}{\mathcal F}\]

In words: The adjoint map rewrites a twist in another frame; a twist paired with a wrench gives the power.

  • 𝒱a the twist written in {a}
  • [AdT] adjoint representation of T
  • Tab configuration of {b} in {a}
  • 𝒱b body twist (in {b})
  • P power
  • 𝒱 twist (angular, linear velocity)
  • ℱ wrench (moment and force)

Premultiplying, R·Rsb, rotates about an axis of the fixed frame {s}; postmultiplying, Rsb·R, rotates about an axis of the body frame {b}. Exponential coordinates are singular at θ = π.

\[\begin{gathered}{}[\class{sym-Ad}{\mathrm{Ad}}_\class{sym-T}{T}]=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\\class{sym-pxy3}{ p_y}&\cos\class{sym-th3}{\theta}&-\sin\class{sym-th3}{\theta}\\ -\class{sym-pxy3}{p_x}&\sin\class{sym-th3}{\theta}&\cos\class{sym-th3}{\theta}\end{bmatrix}\\[2pt]\class{sym-Va}{\mathcal V_a}=[\class{sym-Ad}{\mathrm{Ad}}_{\class{sym-T-ab}{T_{ab}}}]\class{sym-Vb}{\mathcal V_b}\end{gathered}\]

In words: In the plane a twist is (ω, vx, vy); the 3×3 adjoint rotates the linear velocity and adds the part due to the offset p.

  • [AdT] adjoint representation of T
  • T homogeneous transformation matrix
  • px, py coordinates of p
  • θ angle (or distance) along the axis
  • 𝒱a the twist written in {a}
  • Tab configuration of {b} in {a}
  • 𝒱b body twist (in {b})

A planar twist is 𝒱 = (ωz, vx, vy). The arrow at each origin is v in that frame: the velocity of the body point that sits at that origin. For T = (R, p) with R = Rot(θ), the adjoint above maps twists between frames.

Set the plate's twist and push on it with a force. The twist and wrench change when you move the plate or switch frames. The power 𝒱Tℱ does not.

Body twist 𝒱b = (ωz, vx, vy)

Paused
[AdTsb] =

TryDrag the plate around and rotate it. Every entry of 𝒱s and ℱs changes, but the power column stays the same in both frames.
Same twist and wrench in two frames, and the power they share Eq. 3.83Eq. 3.94Eq. 3.95
\[\begin{gathered}\class{sym-Vs}{\mathcal V_s}=[\class{sym-Ad}{\mathrm{Ad}}_{\class{sym-T-sb}{T_{sb}}}]\class{sym-Vb}{\mathcal V_b},\qquad\class{sym-Fb}{ \mathcal F_b}=[\class{sym-Ad}{\mathrm{Ad}}_{\class{sym-T-sb}{T_{sb}}}]^{\mathsf T}\class{sym-Fs}{\mathcal F_s}\\[2pt]\class{sym-Vb}{\mathcal V_b}^{\mathsf T}\class{sym-Fb}{\mathcal F_b}=\class{sym-Vs}{\mathcal V_s}^{\mathsf T}\class{sym-Fs}{\mathcal F_s}\end{gathered}\]

In words: The same motion and the same wrench, written in {s} or in {b}, give the same power in either frame.

  • 𝒱s spatial twist (in {s})
  • [AdT] adjoint representation of T
  • Tsb configuration of {b} in {s}
  • 𝒱b body twist (in {b})
  • ℱb wrench written in {b}
  • ℱs wrench written in {s}

In the plane a twist is 𝒱 = (ωz, vx, vy) and a wrench is ℱ = (mz, fx, fy), with m = r × f (Section 3.4). vs is the velocity of the body point at the origin of {s}, imagining the plate to be infinitely large (Eq. 3.73).

Every body point moves with v = vs + ω × x, and the point that stands still is the center of rotation (CoR) at (−vy/ωz, vx/ωz) (Section 12.1.6). The 3×3 [AdTsb] is the planar form of the 6×6 matrix in Eq. (3.83).

Each rotation R maps to one point ω̂θ, the exponential coordinates from the matrix logarithm. At θ = π the point hits the surface and reappears at the opposite point.

R = Rot(ẑ, α) Rot(ŷ, β) Rot(x̂, γ), Eq. (B.8): roll about the fixed x̂-axis, then pitch about ŷ, then yaw about ẑ.

Matrix logarithm of a rotation

§3.2.3.3Eqs. 3.58–3.61Our choice: case (b) formula
  1. If \(\class{sym-R}{R}=\class{sym-Ieye}{I}\) then \(\class{sym-th3}{\theta}=0\) and \(\class{sym-omegahat}{\hat\omega}\) is undefined.
  2. If \(\class{sym-tr}{\operatorname{tr}}\class{sym-R}{R}=-1\) then \(\class{sym-th3}{\theta}=\pi\). Set \(\class{sym-omegahat}{\hat\omega}\) to any feasible one of Eqs. (3.58)–(3.60), for example \(\class{sym-omegahat}{\hat\omega}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2(1+\class{sym-rij}{r_{33}})}}(\class{sym-rij}{r_{13}},\,\class{sym-rij}{r_{23}},\,1+\class{sym-rij}{r_{33}})\). If \(\class{sym-omegahat}{\hat\omega}\) is a solution, so is \(-\class{sym-omegahat}{\hat\omega}\).
  3. Otherwise \(\class{sym-th3}{\theta}=\cos^{-1}\!\big(\tfrac12(\class{sym-tr}{\operatorname{tr}}\class{sym-R}{R}-1)\big)\in[0,\pi)\) and \(\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-omegahat}{\hat\omega}\class{sym-brk}{]}=\frac{1}{2\sin\class{sym-th3}{\theta}}(\class{sym-R}{R}-\class{sym-R}{R}^{\mathsf T})\), Eq. (3.61). This uses \(\class{sym-tr}{\operatorname{tr}}\class{sym-R}{R}=1+2\cos\class{sym-th3}{\theta}\), Eq. (3.54).

In words: If tr R = −1 the angle is π; otherwise θ comes from the trace of R and [ω̂] from its skew-symmetric part.

  • R rotation matrix
  • I identity matrix
  • θ angle (or distance) along the axis
  • ω̂ unit rotation axis
  • tr trace: sum of diagonal entries
  • rij entries of R
  • [·] bracket: skew-symmetric or se(3) matrix

The highlighted case is the one running now. Inside the ball each rotation has exactly one point. On the surface (θ = π) the two antipodal points r and −r are the same rotation, so a smooth motion that crosses θ = π makes the coordinates jump.

At the center (θ = 0) the axis ω̂ is undefined, and the division by sin θ makes the log numerically sensitive for small θ (Appendix B.3). The book notes that every three-parameter representation of rotation has singularities like these (Section 3.2.3.3, footnote 5). In case (b) this demo picks the formula with the largest denominator.

Part 1 · Ch 4 · Forward kinematics

04From joint angles to where the hand is

Forward kinematics finds the end-effector pose from the joint values. The product of exponentials does it with two frames and one screw axis per joint.

Ch 4 · §4.1–4.21 playgroundQuiz · 3 questions

Orientation

Why this exists

The controller reads joint encoders, but the task is about the hand: is the gripper over the bolt? Forward kinematics computes the end-effector pose T(θ) from θ. The product of exponentials reads one screw axis per joint off the robot at home, with no link frames.

After this you can
  • Write the home pose M and the screw axes 𝒮ᵢ of an open chain.
  • Compute T(θ) with the space form and the body form of the PoE formula.
  • Convert space-frame screw axes to body-frame ones with ℬᵢ = [AdM⁻¹] 𝒮ᵢ.
  • Read a D–H table and see that it gives the same T as PoE.
  • Know what a URDF file describes.
How it connects
← Builds onCh 2Configuration spaceCh 3Rigid-body motions
Leads to →Ch 5Jacobian and staticsCh 6Inverse kinematicsCh 7Closed chainsCh 8Dynamics

Key concepts

Forward kinematics

The map T(θ) from the joint values to the position and orientation of {b} in {s}.

See it in the lab ↗

Open chain

A serial chain of links with no closed loops, where each joint is actuated.

See it in the lab ↗

End-effector frame {b}

A frame attached to some point on the last link.

See it in the lab ↗

Home (zero) position M

The pose of {b} in {s} when all joint values are zero.

See it in the lab ↗

Space screw axis 𝒮ᵢ

The screw axis of joint i written in {s}, with the robot at its zero position.

See it in the lab ↗

Body screw axis ℬᵢ

The screw axis of joint i written in {b}, with the robot at its zero position.

See it in the lab ↗

D–H parameters

Four numbers per link, three for the structure and one for the joint value.

See it in the lab ↗

URDF

The Universal Robot Description Format, a file format for the kinematics and inertia of tree-like robots.

See it in the lab ↗

Where it happens

The robot pipeline, from modeling to motion, with this chapter marked. Use the step buttons to walk through it.

The rule

Space form §4.1.1
\[\class{sym-Tee}{T}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})=\class{sym-expm}{e}^{\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-Si}{\mathcal S_1}\class{sym-brk}{]}\class{sym-theta}{\theta_1}}\class{sym-expm}{e}^{\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-Si}{\mathcal S_2}\class{sym-brk}{]}\class{sym-theta}{\theta_2}}\cdots\class{sym-expm}{ e}^{\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-Si}{\mathcal S_n}\class{sym-brk}{]}\class{sym-theta}{\theta_n}}\class{sym-M}{M}\]
(4.14)

In words: Each joint’s screw motion, the last joint first, carries the home configuration M to the end-effector configuration T(θ).

  • T(θ) end-effector configuration
  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
  • e[·] matrix exponential
  • 𝒮i screw axis of joint i, in {s}
  • [·] bracket: skew-symmetric or se(3) matrix
  • M end-effector configuration at home
Body form §4.1.3
\[\class{sym-Tee}{T}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})=\class{sb-chg}{\class{sym-M}{M}}\,\class{sym-expm}{e}^{[\class{sb-chg}{\class{sym-Bi}{\mathcal B_1}}]\class{sym-theta}{\theta_1}}\cdots\class{sym-expm}{ e}^{[\class{sb-chg}{\class{sym-Bi}{\mathcal B_n}}]\class{sym-theta}{\theta_n}}\]
(4.16)

In words: The same product with M written first and every screw axis expressed in the end-effector frame {b}.

changed from the space form (4.14): M moves to the left, and each axis is written in {b}
  • T(θ) end-effector configuration
  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
  • M end-effector configuration at home
  • e[·] matrix exponential
  • ℬi screw axis of joint i, in {b}
Revolute screw axis §4.1.1
\[\class{sym-S}{\mathcal S}=\begin{bmatrix}\class{sym-omegahat}{\hat\omega}\\ -\class{sym-omegahat}{\hat\omega}\times\class{sym-qpt}{ q}\end{bmatrix}\]

In words: A revolute joint’s screw axis is its unit axis ω̂ together with the linear velocity −ω̂ × q at the origin.

  • 𝒮 screw axis
  • ω̂ unit rotation axis
  • q a point on the axis

A revolute joint about ω̂ through q has 𝒮 = (ω̂, −ω̂×q); a prismatic joint along v̂ has 𝒮 = (0, v̂). PoE needs no link frames, unlike Denavit–Hartenberg (Appendix C).

TryDrag θ₂. The D–H frames {2} and {3} ride on the links, while the PoE screw axes stay where they were at home. The PoE and D–H matrices stay identical.

PoE needs only {s}, {b} and one screw axis per joint, each read off the robot at home. D–H needs 4 numbers per joint, but only after link frames are placed by strict rules: ẑi along joint axis i, x̂i−1 along the common normal from axis i−1 to axis i.

This is the convention of Appendix C (Figure C.1), where link i−1's parameters αi−1, ai−1 sit in Ti−1,i. Other conventions exist. Section C.2 notes that some authors align the joint axis with x̂, and many textbooks (not this one) put Rot(ẑ, θi) first and attach frame {i} at the far end of link i. Always check which one a D–H table assumes.

Equation (C.12) turns D–H into PoE: [𝒮i] = (M1⋯Mi)[Ai](M1⋯Mi)−1, with M = M1M2M3. The status line above runs that check live (the −90° offset of φ2 is folded into M2).

Part 2 · Ch 5 · Velocity kinematics

05The Jacobian: one matrix for speed, force and singularity

The Jacobian maps joint velocities to the end-effector twist. Its transpose maps end-effector wrenches to joint torques, and where it loses rank the robot is singular.

Ch 5 · §5.1–5.41 playgroundQuiz · 3 questions

Orientation

Why this exists

To wipe a table or push on a wall, a robot must know how fast its hand moves and how hard it pushes. One configuration-dependent matrix, the Jacobian, answers both, and also shows where the hand loses a direction of motion.

After this you can
  • Build Js and Jb column by column from the PoE screw axes.
  • Convert between them with Js = [AdTsb] Jb.
  • Find the joint torques needed to apply a wrench with τ = JᵀF.
  • Recognize singular configurations as places where J is not full rank.
  • Read manipulability and force ellipsoids, and compute a measure such as μ₁.
How it connects
← Builds onCh 3Rigid-body motionsCh 4Forward kinematics
Leads to →Ch 6Inverse kinematicsCh 7Closed chainsCh 8DynamicsCh 11Robot control

Key concepts

Jacobian J(θ)

The matrix that maps joint velocities θ̇ to the end-effector twist 𝒱 at configuration θ.

See it in the lab ↗

Space Jacobian

The Jacobian whose columns are joint screw axes in {s} at the current configuration.

See it in the lab ↗

Body Jacobian

The Jacobian whose columns are joint screw axes in {b} at the current configuration.

See it in the lab ↗

Kinematic singularity

A configuration where the rank of the Jacobian is not maximal.

See it in the lab ↗

Redundant robot

A robot with more joints than the task needs, so it has motions that leave the end-effector still.

See it in the lab ↗

Statics

The balance, at rest, between joint torques and the wrench at the end-effector, from equal power at both ends.

See it in the lab ↗

Manipulability ellipsoid

The image of unit joint speeds. Its axes come from the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of JJᵀ.

See it in the lab ↗

Force ellipsoid

The same construction with (JJᵀ)⁻¹: long where the hand pushes easily and short where it moves easily.

See it in the lab ↗

Where it happens

The robot pipeline, from modeling to motion, with this chapter marked. Use the step buttons to walk through it.

Worked example

Build Js for the 3R arm, column by column

Ch 5 · §5.1.1
§5.1.1Def. 5.1Eq. 5.11Our choice: the Ch 4 armSimplified: planar
Space Jacobian of the planar 3R arm Eq. 5.11
Js(θ) = 11100.5001.2730−0.866−1.073
rows: ωz, vx, vy
𝒱s = Jsθ̇ = (1, 1.273, −1.073) for θ̇ = (0, 0, 1)

In words: Column i is joint i’s screw axis at the current configuration; Js times the joint rates gives the spatial twist.

  • Js space Jacobian
  • θ joint angles
  • ωz angular velocity about ẑ
  • vx, vy linear velocity in the plane
  • 𝒱s spatial twist (in {s})
  • θ̇ joint velocities

Given. The Ch 4 arm: L = (1, 0.8, 0.5) m, θ = (30°, 45°, −60°). A revolute joint at (x, y) has planar screw (1, y, −x).

Column 1. Joint 1 sits at the origin and nothing moves it, so Js1 = 𝒮₁ = (1, 0, 0).

Column 2. Joint 1 has carried joint 2 to (0.866, 0.500), so Js2 = (1, 0.500, −0.866).

Column 3. Joints 1 and 2 have carried joint 3 to (1.073, 1.273), so Js3 = (1, 1.273, −1.073).

Result. For θ̇ = (0, 0, 1) rad/s, 𝒱s = Js3. The tip at (1.556, 1.402) moves at vs + ω × p = (−0.129, 0.483) m/s.

Space and body Jacobian, column i §5.1.1–5.1.2
Space
\[\class{sym-Vs}{\mathcal V_s}=\class{sym-Js}{J_s}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})\,\class{sym-thetad}{\dot{\theta}},\quad\class{sym-Jsi}{ J_{si}}=[\class{sym-Ad}{\mathrm{Ad}}_{\class{sym-expm}{e}^{\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-Si}{\mathcal S_1}\class{sym-brk}{]}\class{sym-theta}{\theta_1}}\cdots\class{sym-expm}{ e}^{\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-Si}{\mathcal S_{i-1}}\class{sym-brk}{]}\class{sym-theta}{\theta_{i-1}}}}]\,\class{sym-Si}{\mathcal S_i}\]
(5.11)

In words: Joint velocities times the space Jacobian give the spatial twist; column i is joint i’s screw axis, moved by the joints before it.

Body
\[\class{sym-Vb}{\mathcal V_b}=\class{sym-Jb}{J_b}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})\,\class{sym-thetad}{\dot{\theta}},\quad\class{sym-Jbi}{ J_{bi}}=[\class{sym-Ad}{\mathrm{Ad}}_{\class{sb-chg}{\class{sym-expm}{e}^{-\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-Bi}{\mathcal B_n}\class{sym-brk}{]}\class{sym-theta}{\theta_n}}\cdots\class{sym-expm}{ e}^{-\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-Bi}{\mathcal B_{i+1}}\class{sym-brk}{]}\class{sym-theta}{\theta_{i+1}}}}}]\,\class{sb-chg}{\class{sym-Bi}{\mathcal B_i}}\]
(5.18)

In words: The body Jacobian gives the body twist; its column i is ℬi, moved by the joints after joint i.

changed term
  • 𝒱s spatial twist (in {s})
  • Js space Jacobian
  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
  • θ̇ joint velocities
  • Jsi column i of Js
  • [AdT] adjoint representation of T
  • e[·] matrix exponential
  • 𝒮i screw axis of joint i, in {s}
  • [·] bracket: skew-symmetric or se(3) matrix
  • 𝒱b body twist (in {b})
  • Jb body Jacobian
  • Jbi column i of Jb
  • ℬi screw axis of joint i, in {b}
Statics §5.2
\[\class{sym-tau}{\tau}=\class{sym-J}{J}^{\mathsf T}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})\,\class{sym-F}{\mathcal F}\]
(5.26)

In words: The joint torques that resist a wrench at the end-effector are the transposed Jacobian times that wrench.

  • τ joint torques and forces
  • J Jacobian
  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
  • ℱ wrench (moment and force)
Ellipsoids and a manipulability measure §5.4
\[\class{sym-Amanip}{A}=\class{sym-J}{J}\class{sym-J}{J}^{\mathsf T},\quad\class{sym-Bforce}{ B}=\class{sym-Amanip}{A}^{-1},\quad\class{sym-mu}{ \mu_1}=\sqrt{\class{sym-lam}{\lambda_{\max}}(\class{sym-Amanip}{A})/\class{sym-lam}{\lambda_{\min}}(\class{sym-Amanip}{A})}\ \ge 1\]

In words: A = JJT shapes the manipulability ellipsoid and B = A−1 the force ellipsoid; μ1 near 1 means nearly isotropic.

  • A JJT, shape of the ellipsoid
  • J Jacobian
  • B A−1, force-ellipsoid matrix
  • μ1, μ2, μ3 manipulability measures
  • λi eigenvalues of A

The body column uses the screw axes ℬᵢ in {b} and the joints after i; the two Jacobians are related by Js = [AdTsb]Jb.

Part 2 · Ch 6 · Inverse kinematics

06Given where the hand should be, find the joints

Inverse kinematics finds joint values that put the end-effector at a desired pose. There may be several solutions, infinitely many, or none.

Ch 6 · §6.1–6.31 playgroundQuiz · 3 questions

Orientation

Why this exists

Tasks are stated for the hand, but motors understand joint values. Inverse kinematics maps a desired pose T_sd back to θ. A pose may have several solutions, infinitely many, or none, so the chapter gives closed-form solutions and an iterative Newton–Raphson method.

After this you can
  • Explain why IK can have zero, one, several or infinitely many solutions.
  • Solve a 2R arm by hand; split a PUMA-type arm into position and orientation.
  • Run Newton–Raphson IK with the body Jacobian and the error twist 𝒱b.
  • Pick J⁻¹ or a right or left pseudoinverse from n joints and m task coordinates.
  • Find joint velocities θ̇ that produce a desired end-effector twist.
How it connects
← Builds onCh 4Forward kinematicsCh 5Jacobian and staticsCh 3Rigid-body motionsCh 2Configuration space
Leads to →Ch 7Closed chainsCh 9Trajectory generationCh 11Robot controlCh 13Wheeled mobile robots

Key concepts

Inverse kinematics

Given a desired end-effector configuration X ∈ SE(3), find the joint values θ with T(θ) = X.

See it in the lab ↗

Workspace

The set of end-effector configurations the robot can reach. Outside it, IK has no solution.

See it in the lab ↗

Elbow-up / elbow-down

The two solutions of a 2R arm for an interior point, also called lefty and righty.

See it in the lab ↗

Wrist center

The point where the last three joint axes meet. It lets the problem split into position and orientation parts.

See it in the lab ↗

atan2(y, x)

The four-quadrant arctangent. It returns the angle to (x, y) in (−π, π].

See it in the lab ↗

Initial guess θ⁰

The starting point of Newton–Raphson. The method usually finds the solution closest to it.

See it in the lab ↗

Error twist 𝒱b

The twist that takes the current pose Tsb(θⁱ) to Tsd in one second, from [𝒱b] = log(Tsb⁻¹Tsd).

See it in the lab ↗

Pseudoinverse J†

The generalized inverse of a non-square or singular J. It gives the minimum-norm or least-squares solution of Jθ̇ = 𝒱.

See it in the lab ↗

Where it happens

The robot pipeline, from modeling to motion, with this chapter marked. Use the step buttons to walk through it.

The rule

Hover a symbol to light it up in every equation and diagram of this chapter.

Analytic 2R elbow angle, law of cosines §6.1.1
\[\cos\class{sym-theta}{\theta_2}=\frac{\class{sym-x6}{x}^2+\class{sym-y6}{y}^2-\class{sym-Li}{L_1}^2-\class{sym-Li}{L_2}^2}{2\class{sym-Li}{L_1}\class{sym-Li}{L_2}}\]

In words: The law of cosines gives cos θ2 from the target’s distance; the two signs of θ2 are the righty and lefty solutions.

  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
  • x target x-coordinate of the tip
  • y target y-coordinate of the tip
  • Li link lengths
Newton–Raphson, from J⁻¹ to the body twist §6.2
Before
\[\class{sym-Delta}{\Delta}\class{sym-theta}{\theta}=\class{sb-chg}{\class{sym-J}{J}^{-1}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta}^0)}\big(\class{sb-chg}{\class{sym-xd}{x_d}-\class{sym-fk}{f}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta}^0)}\big)\]
(6.5)

In words: Linearize f at the guess θ0 and step by the joint change that would remove the coordinate error.

After
\[\class{sym-theta}{\theta}^{i+1}=\class{sym-theta}{\theta}^i+\class{sb-chg}{\class{sym-Jbdag}{J_b^{\dagger}}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta}^i)\,\class{sym-Vb}{\mathcal V_b}},\quad \class{sb-new}{\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-Vb}{\mathcal V_b}\class{sym-brk}{]}=\class{sym-logm}{\log}\big(\class{sym-T-sb}{T_{sb}}^{-1}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta}^i)\,\class{sym-T-sd}{T_{sd}}\big)}\]

In words: Each iteration adds Jb† times the body twist that would carry Tsb(θi) to Tsd.

new termchanged term
  • Δ small change of
  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
  • J Jacobian
  • xd desired end-effector coordinates
  • f(θ) forward kinematics map
  • Jb† pseudoinverse of the body Jacobian
  • 𝒱b body twist (in {b})
  • [·] bracket: skew-symmetric or se(3) matrix
  • log matrix logarithm
  • Tsb configuration of {b} in {s}
  • Tsd desired end-effector configuration
Pseudoinverse of a fat, full-rank J §6.2.2
\[\class{sym-Jdag}{J^{\dagger}}=\class{sym-J}{J}^{\mathsf T}(\class{sym-J}{J}\class{sym-J}{J}^{\mathsf T})^{-1}\]

In words: For a full-rank J with more joints than coordinates, J† gives the joint change of smallest size that works.

  • J† pseudoinverse of the Jacobian
  • J Jacobian

Arms whose last three joint axes meet at a wrist point, such as PUMA- and Stanford-type arms, have closed-form solutions. Other arms use Newton–Raphson.

Newton–Raphson, step by step

Simplified: planar, position only

Differs from the bookThe demo runs the position-only version, e = xd − f(θ), θ ← θ + J⁻¹e. It adds small damping near singularities and caps each step; the book's loop has neither.

Part 2 · Ch 7 · Closed chains

07When links form loops

Closed chains contain loops, such as the four-bar and the Stewart–Gough platform. Their inverse kinematics is often direct, while their forward kinematics is hard.

Ch 7 · §7.1–7.31 playgroundQuiz · 3 questions

Orientation

Why this exists

Flight simulators and fast pick-and-place robots connect a platform to a base through several legs. The legs share the load, so these parallel mechanisms are stiff and light. But the links form loops, only some joints have motors, and loop-closure equations tie the joints together.

After this you can
  • Write the loop-closure equations of a simple closed chain.
  • Compute Stewart–Gough leg lengths from a pose; explain why the reverse has many answers.
  • Recognize the two assembly modes of a four-bar linkage.
  • Find the passive joint rates and the Jacobian from Haq̇a + Hpq̇p = 0.
  • Tell configuration-space, actuator and end-effector singularities apart.
How it connects
← Builds onCh 2Configuration spaceCh 4Forward kinematicsCh 5Jacobian and staticsCh 6Inverse kinematics
Leads to →Ch 8DynamicsCh 11Robot control

Key concepts

Closed chain

Any kinematic chain that contains one or more loops.

See it in the lab ↗

Parallel mechanism

A closed chain with a fixed and a moving platform connected by several legs.

See it in the lab ↗

Passive joint

A joint with no actuator. Its value is set by the loop constraints.

See it in the lab ↗

Loop-closure constraint

An equation the joint variables must satisfy so each loop stays closed.

See it in the lab ↗

Assembly mode

One of the distinct ways a closed chain can be put together for the same actuator values.

See it in the lab ↗

Configuration-space singularity

A self-intersection of the C-space surface. It does not depend on which joints are actuated.

See it in the lab ↗

Actuator singularity

The actuated joints cannot be moved independently, or locking them fails to make the mechanism rigid.

See it in the lab ↗

End-effector singularity

The end-effector loses one or more directions of motion. It depends on where the end-effector frame is placed.

See it in the lab ↗

Where it happens

The robot pipeline, from modeling to motion, with this chapter marked. Use the step buttons to walk through it.

Worked example

Leg lengths of a 3×RPR platform

Ch 7 · §7.1.1
§7.1.1Fig. 7.2Our choice: dimensions and pose
Leg vectors and lengths Eq. 7.1Eq. 7.2
di = p + Rsbbi − ai
si = ‖di‖
s = (1.942, 2.002, 1.471)

In words: Each leg vector runs from base point ai to the moved platform point p + Rsbbi; its length is the joint value si.

  • di vector along leg i
  • p platform position in {s}
  • Rsb platform orientation in {s}
  • bi leg i attachment on the platform
  • ai leg i attachment on the base
  • si length of leg i
  • ‖·‖ length of a vector

Given. Base joints a₁ = (0, 0), a₂ = (4, 0), a₃ = (2, 3.5). The platform, a unit triangle, is at p = (2, 1.5) with φ = 20°.

Rotate b₁ into {s}. In {b}, b₁ = (−0.500, −0.289). Rotating by φ = 20° gives Rsbb₁ = (−0.371, −0.442).

Leg vector. d₁ = p + Rsbb₁ − a₁ = (1.629, 1.058), so the first leg length is s₁ = ‖d₁‖ = 1.942.

All legs. The same formula gives s₂ = 2.002 and s₃ = 1.471. Inverse kinematics is direct: one pose gives one set of leg lengths.

The hard direction. Going back from (s₁, s₂, s₃) to the pose needs a sixth-order polynomial, with up to six solutions.

The rule

Hover a symbol to light it up in every equation and diagram of this chapter.

Stewart–Gough leg i: base point aᵢ, platform point bᵢ §7.1.2
\[\class{sym-di}{d_i} =\class{sym-p7}{ p}+\class{sym-R7}{R}\,\class{sym-bi}{b_i} -\class{sym-ai}{ a_i},\qquad\class{sym-si}{ s_i}=\lVert\class{sym-di}{ d_i}\rVert\]

In words: Leg i runs from the base point ai to the moved platform point p + Rbi; its length si is the actuated joint.

  • di vector along leg i
  • p platform position in {s}
  • R platform orientation in {s}
  • bi leg i attachment on the platform
  • ai leg i attachment on the base
  • si length of leg i

Closed chains add actuator and configuration-space singularities to end-effector ones. Stewart–Gough platforms serve as motion simulators and six-axis force–torque sensors.

This is the 6×SPS design of Section 7.1.2: prismatic legs are actuated, spherical joints are passive. Inverse kinematics has one answer per pose.

Forward kinematics runs the other way: given the six si, solve si2 = (p + Rbi − ai)T(p + Rbi − ai) together with RTR = I, 12 equations in 12 unknowns. It usually has several solutions, and the most general platform can have up to 40 (Section 7.5).

The 6-6 joint layout, dimensions and stroke limits here are illustrative choices, not values from the book.

Part 3 · Ch 8 · Open-chain dynamics

08Forces in, motion out

Dynamics links joint torques to motion. Forward dynamics finds accelerations from torques; inverse dynamics finds the torques a desired motion needs.

Ch 8 · §8.1–8.92 playgroundsQuiz · 3 questions

Orientation

Why this exists

Kinematics says where the arm is, not how hard the motors must push. Gravity, inertia and the coupling between links all pull on each joint. A dynamic model links joint torques τ to the motion θ̈ they produce, for controllers and for simulators.

After this you can
  • Derive the equations of motion of a simple arm from its kinetic and potential energy.
  • Read τ = M(θ)θ̈ + c(θ, θ̇) + g(θ) and say what each term does.
  • Run the recursive Newton–Euler algorithm: velocities out, wrenches back.
  • Simulate an arm by solving for θ̈ and integrating it forward in time.
  • Estimate the apparent inertia a geared motor adds at a joint.
How it connects
← Builds onCh 3Rigid-body motionsCh 4Forward kinematicsCh 5Jacobian and statics
Leads to →Ch 9Trajectory generationCh 11Robot controlCh 12Grasping

Key concepts

Forward dynamics

Find the joint accelerations θ̈ produced by given joint torques τ.

See it in the lab ↗

Inverse dynamics

Find the joint torques τ needed to produce given accelerations θ̈.

See it in the lab ↗

Lagrangian ℒ

Kinetic minus potential energy, ℒ(θ, θ̇) = K − P.

See it in the lab ↗

Mass matrix M(θ)

The n × n symmetric positive-definite matrix with kinetic energy K = ½θ̇ᵀM(θ)θ̇.

See it in the lab ↗

Coriolis and centripetal c(θ, θ̇)

Coriolis and centripetal forces, quadratic in the joint velocities.

See it in the lab ↗

Gravity torque g(θ)

The joint torques needed to hold the arm against gravity.

See it in the lab ↗

Rotational inertia Ib

The 3 × 3 symmetric positive-definite matrix describing how a body's mass is spread about its center of mass.

See it in the lab ↗

Spatial inertia 𝒢b

The 6 × 6 matrix built from Ib and mass m, which links a body's twist to its momentum.

See it in the lab ↗

Where it happens

The robot pipeline, from modeling to motion, with this chapter marked. Use the step buttons to walk through it.

The rule

Hover a symbol to light it up in every equation and diagram of this chapter.

Euler–Lagrange, with ℒ = 𝒦 − 𝒫 §8.1.1
\[\class{sym-tau}{\tau}=\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial\class{sym-Lag}{ \mathcal L}}{\partial\class{sym-thetad}{\dot\theta}}-\frac{\partial\class{sym-Lag}{\mathcal L}}{\partial\class{sym-theta}{\theta}}\]
(8.3)

In words: The joint torques are the time derivative of ∂ℒ/∂θ̇ minus ∂ℒ/∂θ, where ℒ is kinetic minus potential energy.

  • τ joint torques and forces
  • ℒ Lagrangian: kinetic minus potential
  • θ̇ joint velocities
  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
Inverse and forward dynamics, h = c + g §8.1, §8.5
Inverse
\[\class{sym-tau}{\tau}=\class{sym-Mth}{M}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})\class{sym-thetadd}{\ddot{\theta}}+\class{sym-hdyn}{h}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta},\class{sym-thetad}{\dot\theta})\]
(8.1)

In words: Inverse dynamics: the torques for a given acceleration are the mass matrix times that acceleration plus the velocity and gravity terms.

Forward
\[\class{sym-thetadd}{\ddot{\theta}}=\class{sb-chg}{\class{sym-Mth}{M}^{-1}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})}\big(\class{sb-chg}{\class{sym-tau}{\tau}-\class{sym-hdyn}{h}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta},\class{sym-thetad}{\dot\theta})}\big)\]
(8.2)

In words: Forward dynamics: the same equation solved for the acceleration that given torques produce; integrating it simulates the robot.

changed term
  • τ joint torques and forces
  • M(θ) mass matrix
  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
  • θ̈ joint accelerations
  • h(θ, θ̇) gravity plus quadratic velocity terms
  • θ̇ joint velocities
One rigid body, body frame §8.2.2
\[\class{sym-Fb}{\mathcal F_b}=\class{sym-G}{\mathcal G_b}\class{sym-Vdotb}{\dot{\mathcal V}_b}-[\class{sym-ad}{\mathrm{ad}}_{\class{sym-Vb}{\mathcal V_b}}]^{\mathsf T}\class{sym-G}{\mathcal G_b}\class{sym-Vb}{\mathcal V_b}\]
(8.40)

In words: The wrench on one rigid body is its spatial inertia times its acceleration minus a velocity-product term, all in {b}.

  • ℱb wrench written in {b}
  • 𝒢b spatial inertia matrix in {b}
  • 𝒱̇b rate of change of 𝒱b
  • [ad𝒱] Lie bracket matrix of a twist
  • 𝒱b body twist (in {b})

The Lagrangian route starts from energy; Newton–Euler applies f = ma to each link. Both give the same τ. c(θ, θ̇) is quadratic in the velocities.

The Lagrangian route differentiates the energy of the whole arm. The Newton–Euler route applies f = ma one link at a time, out and back along the chain.

Interactive

Check both routes on the 2R arm

Eq. 8.9Eqs. 8.50–8.54

Set any state (θ, θ̇, θ̈). The closed form of Eq. 8.9 and the recursion of Eqs. 8.50–8.54 return the same torques.

TrySet both velocities to 0: c(θ, θ̇) vanishes and only M(θ)θ̈ + g(θ) is left. The twists on the right become zero too.

Same 2R arm as the forward-dynamics demo: point masses m₁ = m₂ = 1 kg at the link tips, L₁ = L₂ = 1 m, g = 9.81 m/s² along −ŷ (Fig. 8.1). For Newton–Euler, frame {i} sits at mass i and is aligned with {0} at θ = 0, so M1,0 and M2,1 are pure translations by −L₁ and −L₂ along x̂.

The screw axes are 𝒜₁ = (0, 0, 1, 0, L₁, 0) and 𝒜₂ = (0, 0, 1, 0, L₂, 0). A point mass has zero rotational inertia, so 𝒢ᵢ = diag(0, 0, 0, mᵢ, mᵢ, mᵢ). Gravity enters as a base acceleration 𝒱̇₀ = (0, 0, 0, 0, 9.81, 0), and ℱ₃ = ℱtip = 0.

Twists are shown as (ωz; vx, vy) and wrenches as (mz; fx, fy) in each link frame. The other components are zero for this planar arm.

Part 3 · Ch 9 · Trajectory generation

09A path says where, a time scaling says when

A trajectory is a path, which says where, combined with a time scaling, which says when. Good time scalings stay smooth and within limits.

Ch 9 · §9.1–9.41 playgroundQuiz · 3 questions

Orientation

Why this exists

A user should not program every joint angle at every instant. They give a start, a goal or a few timed via points, and the robot fills in a smooth motion that stays within the motors' limits.

After this you can
  • Write a trajectory as a path composed with a time scaling, θ(s(t)).
  • Build straight-line paths in joint space and in task space.
  • Choose between cubic, quintic, trapezoidal and S-curve time scalings.
  • Interpolate timed via points with cubic or quintic segments.
  • Explain how the (s, ṡ) phase plane gives the time-optimal motion along a path.
How it connects
← Builds onCh 2Configuration spaceCh 3Rigid-body motionsCh 6Inverse kinematicsCh 8Dynamics
Leads to →Ch 10Motion planningCh 11Robot controlCh 13Wheeled mobile robots

Key concepts

Trajectory

A specification of the robot's configuration as a function of time, θ(t) for t ∈ [0, T].

See it in the lab ↗

Path

A purely geometric curve θ(s), s ∈ [0, 1], through configuration space.

See it in the lab ↗

Time scaling s(t)

A function from [0, T] to [0, 1] that sets when each point of the path is reached.

See it in the lab ↗

Via point

An intermediate state the trajectory must pass through at a given time.

See it in the lab ↗

Jerk

The time derivative of acceleration. A step in acceleration means infinite jerk.

See it in the lab ↗

Phase plane (s, ṡ)

The plane of path position and path speed, where a time scaling is a curve.

See it in the lab ↗

Acceleration bounds L, U

The minimum and maximum path accelerations s̈ allowed by the actuator limits at a state.

See it in the lab ↗

Velocity limit curve

The boundary in the phase plane above which L > U, so no admissible s̈ exists.

See it in the lab ↗

Where it happens

The robot pipeline, from modeling to motion, with this chapter marked. Use the step buttons to walk through it.

The rule

Hover a symbol to light it up in every equation and diagram of this chapter.

Straight-line joint path §9.2.1
\[\class{sym-theta}{\theta}(\class{sym-s}{s})=\class{sym-thstart}{\theta_{\text{start}}}+\class{sym-s}{s}\,(\class{sym-thend}{\theta_{\text{end}}}-\class{sym-thstart}{\theta_{\text{start}}})\]
(9.3)

In words: The path moves along a straight line from θstart to θend as s goes from 0 to 1.

  • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
  • s path parameter, 0 to 1
  • θstart start configuration
  • θend end configuration
Cubic to quintic time scaling §9.2.2.1
Cubic
\[\class{sym-s}{s}(\class{sym-t}{t})=\class{sb-chg}{3\frac{\class{sym-t}{t}^2}{\class{sym-Tmot}{T}^2}-2\frac{\class{sym-t}{t}^3}{\class{sym-Tmot}{T}^3}}\]

In words: A cubic time scaling leaves s = 0 at rest and reaches s = 1 at rest at time T.

Quintic
\[\class{sym-s}{s}(\class{sym-t}{t})=\class{sb-chg}{10\Big(\frac\class{sym-t}{ t}\class{sym-Tmot}{T}\Big)^3-15\Big(\frac\class{sym-t}{ t}\class{sym-Tmot}{T}\Big)^4+6\Big(\frac\class{sym-t}{ t}\class{sym-Tmot}{T}\Big)^5}\]

In words: The quintic also starts and ends with zero acceleration, so the jerk stays finite.

changed term
  • s path parameter, 0 to 1
  • t time
  • T total motion time
Task-space screw path §9.2.1
\[\class{sym-X9}{X}(\class{sym-s}{s})=\class{sym-Xstart}{X_{\text{start}}}\class{sym-expm}{\exp}\!\big(\class{sym-logm}{\log}(\class{sym-Xstart}{X_{\text{start}}}^{-1}\class{sym-Xend}{X_{\text{end}}})\,\class{sym-s}{s}\big)\]
(9.6)

In words: A straight line in SE(3): the end-effector follows one constant screw motion from Xstart to Xend.

  • X(s) end-effector configuration on the path
  • s path parameter, 0 to 1
  • Xstart start end-effector configuration
  • e[·] matrix exponential
  • log matrix logarithm
  • Xend end end-effector configuration

The quintic also sets s̈ = 0 at both ends. Via points are joined by one cubic per segment, matching position and velocity at each via time.

T = 1 s

Interactive

Time-optimal time scaling in the phase plane

Ch 9 · §9.4Fig. 9.11Our choice: paths, integration in ṡ²

TryPick Near base: the tip passes 0.24 m from joint 1 and the solution needs several switches. Hover the phase plane to see the motion cone at any state.
Changing τmax or the path recomputes the solution.
Dynamics
\(\class{sym-m9}{ m}(\class{sym-s}{s})\class{sym-sddot}{\ddot s}+\class{sym-c9}{c}(\class{sym-s}{s})\class{sym-sdot}{\dot s}^2+\class{sym-g9}{g}(\class{sym-s}{s})=\class{sym-tau}{\tau} \)
Eq. 9.33

In words: Along a fixed path the robot’s dynamics reduce to one scalar equation in s, ṡ and s̈ that gives the joint torques.

Limits
\(\class{sym-L9}{ L}(\class{sym-s}{s},\class{sym-sdot}{\dot s})\le\class{sym-sddot}{\ddot s}\le\class{sym-U9}{ U}(\class{sym-s}{s},\class{sym-sdot}{\dot s}) \)
Eq. 9.37

In words: Actuator limits bound the path acceleration s̈ between L and U, both depending on the state (s, ṡ).

Time
\(\class{sym-Tmot}{ T}=\int_0^1\class{sym-sdot}{ \dot s}^{-1}(\class{sym-s}{s})\,ds \)
Eq. 9.39

In words: The motion time is the integral of 1/ṡ over the path, so the fastest time scaling keeps ṡ as large as the limits allow.

  • m(s) effective inertia along the path
  • s path parameter, 0 to 1
  • s̈ path acceleration
  • c(s) quadratic velocity term along the path
  • ṡ path velocity
  • g(s) gravity term along the path
  • τ joint torques and forces
  • L(s, ṡ) minimum feasible path acceleration
  • U(s, ṡ) maximum feasible path acceleration
  • T total motion time

Each joint limit gives a band for s̈ (Eq. 9.36). L is the largest lower bound and U the smallest upper bound. The curves follow the time-scaling algorithm of Section 9.4.2. F integrates L backward from (1, 0). Each Ai integrates U forward.

When Ai pierces the velocity limit curve, a binary search on ṡ finds the point where a deceleration curve touches it, and the solution switches there. The Near base path needs several switches.

The integration runs in x = ṡ², where dx/ds = 2s̈, so curves can start from ṡ = 0 (not from the book). Both joints share the same limit, |τ₁|, |τ₂| ≤ τmax.

Part 3 · Ch 10 · Motion planning

10Finding a way through clutter

Motion planning finds a collision-free motion from start to goal. The search happens in C-space, where obstacles become C-obstacles.

Ch 10 · §10.1–10.82 playgroundsQuiz · 3 questions

Orientation

Why this exists

Moving a part from a bin to a fixture without hitting anything needs more than inverse kinematics. Motion planning finds a collision-free route that respects joint and actuator limits. It searches C-space, where each obstacle becomes a C-obstacle and the robot shrinks to a point.

After this you can
  • State a planning problem in C-space, with C = Cfree ∪ Cobs.
  • Run A* on a grid and explain why an optimistic heuristic keeps the path optimal.
  • Build an RRT or a PRM, and say when each fits: single or many queries.
  • Use a virtual potential field and recognize when it gets stuck in a local minimum.
  • Compare planners by completeness, cost and path quality, and smooth a jerky path.
How it connects
← Builds onCh 2Configuration spaceCh 4Forward kinematicsCh 9Trajectory generation
Leads to →Ch 11Robot controlCh 13Wheeled mobile robotsCh 4–11Robot playground

Key concepts

C-obstacle

The set of configurations where the robot touches an obstacle. Together these form Cobs.

See it in the lab ↗

Free space Cfree

The configurations where the robot does not penetrate any obstacle. A path must stay inside it.

See it in the lab ↗

Path vs motion planning

Path planning finds a collision-free geometric path. Motion planning also accounts for dynamics, duration and control limits.

See it in the lab ↗

Resolution-complete

A planner that finds a solution if one exists at the chosen discretization.

See it in the lab ↗

Probabilistically complete

A planner whose chance of finding an existing solution goes to 1 as planning time grows.

See it in the lab ↗

Single vs multiple query

A single-query planner solves one start–goal pair. A multiple-query planner builds a structure, like a roadmap, reused for many.

See it in the lab ↗

Admissible heuristic

A cost-to-go estimate that never overestimates the true cost, so A* returns an optimal path.

See it in the lab ↗

Local minimum

A point where the potential gradient is zero but the goal is not reached, so the robot stops.

See it in the lab ↗

Where it happens

The robot pipeline, from modeling to motion, with this chapter marked. Use the step buttons to walk through it.

The rule

Hover a symbol to light it up in every equation and diagram of this chapter.

Dijkstra to A*: how a node is ranked §10.2.4
Dijkstra
\[\class{sym-est}{\mathtt{est\_total\_cost}}[\class{sym-node}{n}]=\class{sym-past-cost}{\mathtt{past\_cost}}[\class{sym-node}{n}]\]

In words: Dijkstra’s algorithm ranks each open node by the cost of the best path to it found so far.

A*
\[\class{sym-est}{\mathtt{est\_total\_cost}}[\class{sym-node}{n}]=\class{sym-past-cost}{\mathtt{past\_cost}}[\class{sym-node}{n}]+\class{sb-new}{\class{sym-h-cost}{\mathtt{heuristic\_cost\_to\_go}}(\class{sym-node}{n})}\]

In words: A* adds an optimistic estimate of the remaining cost, so the search reaches toward the goal first.

new term
  • est_total_cost estimated cost of the best path
  • n a node of the graph
  • past_cost cost of the best path so far
  • heuristic_cost_to_go optimistic estimate of remaining cost
Potential field and control force §10.6
\[\class{sym-Pq}{\mathcal P}(\class{sym-q}{q})=\tfrac12 (\class{sym-q}{q}-\class{sym-qgoal}{q_{\text{goal}}})^{\mathsf T}\class{sym-K10}{K}(\class{sym-q}{q}-\class{sym-qgoal}{q_{\text{goal}}})+\textstyle\sum\class{sym-Pobs}{ \mathcal P_{\text{obs}}},\quad\class{sym-F10}{ F}=-\frac{\partial\class{sym-Pq}{\mathcal P}}{\partial\class{sym-q}{ q}}\]

In words: A quadratic well pulls q toward qgoal and obstacle potentials push it away; the force is minus the gradient.

  • 𝒫(q) virtual potential field
  • q configuration
  • qgoal goal configuration
  • K gain matrix of the goal potential
  • 𝒫obs potential of an obstacle
  • F(q) force: minus the potential gradient
C-space split §10.2
\[\class{sym-C}{\mathcal C}=\class{sym-Cfree}{\mathcal C_{\text{free}}}\cup\class{sym-Cobs}{\mathcal C_{\text{obs}}}\]

In words: Every configuration is either free or in collision with an obstacle.

  • 𝒞 configuration space (C-space)
  • 𝒞free free space
  • 𝒞obs C-obstacle space

A heuristic that never overestimates keeps A* optimal. Complete planners also report when no path exists, but only simple problems stay practical.

Planner arena: grid A*, PRM and RRT

Ch 10 · §10.4–10.5Alg. 10.3Alg. 10.4Our choice: worlds, parameters

One world, one start and one goal, three planners. Run each planner and compare the results in the table. Drag the start or goal to move them.

PlannerLast runPath lengthNodes / samplesTime×20 success×20 mean length
A* (grid)––––––
PRM––––––
RRT––––––

World 100 × 60, point robot, so C = ℝ². Times include building the grid or roadmap. RRT uses step d = 2.5, a 5% goal bias and a goal set of radius 2.

TryPick Narrow passage and press Run A*: it fails until you add enough grid cells for one to fit inside the gap. Then press Run all ×20 and compare PRM and RRT success rates.

A* uses an 8-connected grid (edge cost 1 or √2 per cell) with the straight-line heuristic. A grid cell counts as free only if no part of it touches an obstacle. PRM samples Cfree uniformly, links each sample to its k nearest neighbors with a straight-line local planner (Algorithm 10.4), then searches the roadmap with A*.

Why the narrow passage is hard

The gap is 2.4 units tall and 20 long, under 1% of the world. A uniform sampler rarely lands inside it, and a PRM needs samples in the gap that can see each other and both sides. Sampling more densely near obstacles can help (Section 10.5.2).

For the grid, a coarse resolution "may miss free paths" (Section 10.4). Any cell taller than the gap touches a wall, so A* fails until the cells fit inside it. That is resolution completeness: A* finds a path if one exists at the chosen resolution.

What to notice

A* returns the same shortest grid path every time. Its cost grows as kn grid points in n dimensions, so it suits only low-dimensional C-spaces. PRM and RRT are probabilistically complete: their success rate rises toward 100% with more samples, and their paths vary run to run.

Sampling planners' paths can be jerky; the book suggests smoothing them afterwards (Section 10.8). It also describes the bidirectional RRT and RRT*, which rewires the tree toward the optimum (Section 10.5.1.4). They are not run here.

Part 4 · Ch 11 · Robot control

11Feedback turns intent into torque

A controller turns a task into actuator commands. Feedback corrects the errors a model can't predict; a model removes the errors you can predict.

Ch 11 · §11.1–11.71 playgroundQuiz · 3 questions

Orientation

Why this exists

Planners say where the joints should be; motors accept only torques or velocities. The controller converts one into the other. Models are never perfect, so feedback measures and corrects the error, while a model used as feedforward supplies the torques you can predict.

After this you can
  • Read overshoot, 2% settling time and steady-state error, and link them to ζ and ωₙ.
  • Tune a PID joint controller and explain why gravity leaves a steady-state error under PD.
  • Write the computed torque law and say what goes wrong when the model is off.
  • Split a contact task into force-controlled and motion-controlled directions.
  • Choose between impedance and admittance control for a given robot.
How it connects
← Builds onCh 8DynamicsCh 5Jacobian and staticsCh 9Trajectory generationCh 3Rigid-body motions
Leads to →Ch 12GraspingCh 13Wheeled mobile robotsCh 4–11Robot playground

Key concepts

Error θe

The difference θd − θ between the desired and the actual joint values.

See it in the lab ↗

Feedforward

Control computed from the desired motion and a model, with no measurement of the error.

See it in the lab ↗

Feedback

Control computed from the measured error, which corrects what the model misses.

See it in the lab ↗

Damping ratio ζ and natural frequency ωₙ

The two numbers of standard second-order error dynamics. ζ sets the overshoot and ωₙ the speed.

See it in the lab ↗

Steady-state error

The error that remains as time goes to infinity.

See it in the lab ↗

Natural constraint

A motion or force the environment fixes, like zero velocity into a rigid wall.

See it in the lab ↗

Artificial constraint

A motion or force the controller chooses in the directions the environment leaves free.

See it in the lab ↗

Impedance

How the end-effector motion changes under disturbance forces. High impedance resists motion, low impedance yields.

See it in the lab ↗

Where it happens

The robot pipeline, from modeling to motion, with this chapter marked. Use the step buttons to walk through it.

The rule

Hover a symbol to light it up in every equation and diagram of this chapter.

Standard second-order error dynamics §11.2.2
\[\class{sym-theddot}{\ddot\theta_e}+2\class{sym-zeta}{\zeta}\class{sym-wn}{\omega_n}\class{sym-thedot}{\dot\theta_e}+\class{sym-wn}{\omega_n}^2\class{sym-the}{\theta_e}=0\]
(11.8)

In words: The joint error behaves like a mass–spring–damper with damping ratio ζ and natural frequency ωn.

  • θ̈e second derivative of joint error
  • ζ damping ratio
  • ωn natural frequency
  • θ̇e rate of joint error
  • θe joint error θd − θ
PID to computed torque §11.4.1
PID
\[\class{sym-tau}{\tau}=\class{sym-Kp}{K_p}\class{sym-the}{\theta_e}+\class{sym-Ki}{K_i}\!\int\!\class{sym-the}{\theta_e}\,dt+\class{sym-Kd}{K_d}\class{sym-thedot}{\dot\theta_e}\]
(11.23)

In words: Torque proportional to the joint error, to its integral and to its derivative.

Computed
\[\class{sym-tau}{\tau}=\class{sb-new}{\class{sym-Mt}{\tilde M}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})}\big(\class{sb-new}{\class{sym-thdesddot}{\ddot\theta_d}}+\class{sym-Kp}{K_p}\class{sym-the}{\theta_e}+\class{sym-Ki}{K_i}\!\int\!\class{sym-the}{\theta_e}\,dt+\class{sym-Kd}{K_d}\class{sym-thedot}{\dot\theta_e}\big)+\class{sb-new}{\class{sym-ht}{\tilde h}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta},\class{sym-thetad}{\dot\theta})}\]
(11.35)

In words: The dynamics model turns the PID-corrected desired acceleration into joint torques, canceling the arm’s own dynamics.

new term

  • Kp proportional gain
  • θe joint error θd − θ
  • Ki integral gain
  • Kd derivative gain
  • θ̇e rate of joint error

Impedance target §11.7
\[\class{sym-Mv}{M}\class{sym-x11dd}{\ddot x}+\class{sym-Bv}{B}\class{sym-x11d}{\dot x}+\class{sym-Kv}{K}\class{sym-x11}{x}=\class{sym-fext}{f_{\text{ext}}}\]

In words: The end-effector should respond like a mass–spring–damper when the environment pushes on it with fext.

  • M virtual mass
  • ẍ end-effector acceleration
  • B virtual damping
  • ẋ end-effector velocity
  • K virtual stiffness
  • x end-effector position
  • fext force applied by the environment

Motion control tracks positions; force control regulates contact force. Hybrid motion–force control does each in different directions, and impedance control sets a virtual spring–damper–mass.

A tip touches a frictionless wall, like chalk on a chalkboard (Sec. 11.6.1). Hybrid pushes with a set force while sliding; impedance acts like a mass–spring–damper pulled 4 cm into the wall.

    Normal n̂ (into the wall)vn = 0fn = fd
    Tangent t̂ (along the wall)ft = 0frictionless: always 0 Nvt = vd(t)

    Hybrid motion–force control with velocity damping Eq. 11.61Eq. 11.54
    \[\begin{aligned}\class{sym-F}{\mathcal F}={}&\class{sym-P11}{P}\,\class{sym-Lamt}{\tilde\Lambda}\big(\class{sym-x11ddd}{\ddot x_d}+\class{sym-Kp}{K_p}\class{sym-xe}{ x_e}+\class{sym-Kd}{K_d}\class{sym-xedot}{\dot x_e}\big)\\&+(\class{sym-Ieye}{I}-\class{sym-P11}{P})\Big(\class{sym-fd}{f_d}+\class{sym-Kfp}{K_{fp}}\class{sym-fe}{f_e}+\class{sym-Kfi}{K_{fi}}\!\int\!\class{sym-fe}{ f_e}\,dt-\class{sym-Kdamp}{K_{\text{damp}}}\class{sym-x11d}{\dot x}\Big)\\\class{sym-P11}{P}={}&\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}\]

    In words: Motion control acts in the directions P leaves free; force control, with velocity damping, acts in the constrained direction I − P.

    • ℱ wrench (moment and force)
    • P projection onto motion-controlled directions
    • Λ̃(θ) model of task-space mass matrix
    • ẍd desired end-effector acceleration
    • Kp proportional gain
    • xe position error
    • Kd derivative gain
    • ẋe velocity error
    • I identity matrix
    • fd desired force

    This is Eq. 11.61 for a planar point, with the velocity damping of Eq. 11.54 added to the force part. With the constraint A = [1 0] (no motion into the wall) and Λ = mI, the projection P of Eq. 11.60 keeps the tangent direction for motion control, and I − P keeps the normal direction for force control. The two controllers never fight.

    Impedance about the reference Eq. 11.64
    \[\class{sym-Mv}{ M}\class{sym-x11dd}{\ddot x}+\class{sym-Bv}{B}\class{sym-x11d}{\dot x}+\class{sym-Kv}{K}(\class{sym-x11}{x}-\class{sym-xref}{x_{\text{ref}}})=\class{sym-fext}{f_{\text{ext}}} \]

    In words: The same mass–spring–damper behavior, with the spring’s rest position at xref.

    • M virtual mass
    • ẍ end-effector acceleration
    • B virtual damping
    • ẋ end-effector velocity
    • K virtual stiffness
    • x end-effector position
    • xref reference (rest) position
    • fext force applied by the environment

    x is measured from the reference, as the book allows. fext is the force the wall applies to the robot. The robot does not control force: the force follows from where the reference sits. In steady state f ≈ K·Δ, where Δ is how far the reference sits inside the wall.

    Impedance control (Eq. 11.65)The robot senses motion x, ẋ and commands joint torques to create the force of Eq. 11.64. It suits a light, backdrivable arm. A very stiff K turns small sensor errors into large torques.
    Admittance control (Eq. 11.66)A wrist load cell senses fext, and the robot commands ẍd = M⁻¹(fext − Bẋ − Kx). It suits a highly geared arm. A very small M turns small forces into large accelerations.

    Simulation detail: in Hybrid mode the tip is a 2 kg point mass (Λ = mI) in a horizontal plane. In Impedance mode the tip moves exactly as Eq. 11.64 says, as an ideal controller would make it. Both use a 0.1 ms integration step.

    Part 4 · Ch 12 · Grasping

    12Holding things: contacts, friction and closure

    Contact kinematics, a friction model and rigid-body dynamics give two tests for a secure grasp: form closure from geometry, force closure with friction.

    Ch 12 · §12.1–12.31 playgroundQuiz · 3 questions

    Orientation

    Why this exists

    Useful work means acting on objects: picking up a bolt, pushing a box, stacking blocks. Everything passes through contacts, so we need to know which motions a contact allows and which forces it can transmit.

    After this you can
    • Write the contact wrench of a point contact and the impenetrability constraint.
    • Label a contact as rolling (R), sliding (S) or breaking (B).
    • Draw a friction cone and decide which contact forces Coulomb friction allows.
    • Test a grasp for first-order form closure and for force closure.
    • Apply contact models to pushing, carrying and the stability of an assembly.
    How it connects
    ← Builds onCh 3Rigid-body motionsCh 5Jacobian and staticsCh 8DynamicsCh 11Robot control
    Leads to →Ch 13Wheeled mobile robotsApp AFormula sheet

    Key concepts

    Contact normal n̂

    The unit vector at the contact, orthogonal to the tangent plane and pointing into body A.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Impenetrability constraint

    The condition ℱᵀ(𝒱A − 𝒱B) ≥ 0 that stops bodies from moving into each other.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Contact mode

    The list of labels (R, S or B) for all contacts of a body.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Friction cone

    The set of contact forces with ft ≤ μ fn. A sliding contact's force lies on its edge.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Wrench cone

    The positive span of all contact wrenches the contacts can transmit.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Positive span

    All combinations of a set of vectors with non-negative coefficients.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Form closure

    The contacts prevent all motion of the body by geometry alone.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Force closure

    The contact wrench cone is the whole wrench space, so the contacts resist any external wrench.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Where it happens

    The robot pipeline, from modeling to motion, with this chapter marked. Use the step buttons to walk through it.

    Worked example

    Can two fingers hold a triangle?

    Ch 12 · §12.2.3
    Fig. 12.22§12.2.3Our choice: contact height
    Friction angle and the two-finger test §12.2.3
    α = tan−1 μ
    line of sight at 30° to each normal
    force closure ⇔ α > 30° ⇔ μ > tan 30° ≈ 0.577

    In words: The friction cone’s half-angle is tan⁻¹ μ; two fingers give force closure when the line between contacts lies inside both cones.

    • α half-angle of the friction cone
    • μ friction coefficient

    Given. Two fingers touch an equilateral triangle on two edges, at the same height. The arrows are the inward contact normals.

    Line of sight. The dashed line joins the contacts. It makes 30° with each normal, because each edge is tilted 60°.

    μ = 0.25. The friction angle is α = tan⁻¹ 0.25 = 14.0°. The line of sight lies outside both cones, so there is no force closure.

    μ = 1. Now α = 45° > 30°. The contacts see each other inside both cones: the four cone edges positively span the planar wrench space.

    Result. The threshold is μ = tan 30° ≈ 0.577. Below it the fingers can't resist every wrench; above it they can, given enough squeeze.

    The rule

    Hover a symbol to light it up in every equation and diagram of this chapter.

    Coulomb friction §12.2
    \[\class{sym-ft}{f_t}\le\class{sym-mufr}{\mu}\class{sym-fn}{ f_n},\qquad\class{sym-alfr}{ \alpha}=\arctan\class{sym-mufr}{\mu}\]

    In words: The contact does not slip while the tangential force is at most μ times the normal force; α is the cone’s half-angle.

    • ft tangential contact force
    • μ friction coefficient
    • fn normal contact force
    • α friction angle (cone half-angle)
    Contact wrench and impenetrability §12.1.2
    \[\class{sym-Fc}{\mathcal F}=\begin{bmatrix}\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-p12}{p}\class{sym-brk}{]}\class{sym-n}{\hat n}\\\class{sym-n}{ \hat n}\end{bmatrix},\qquad\class{sym-Fc}{ \mathcal F}^{\mathsf T}(\class{sym-VA}{\mathcal V_A}-\class{sym-VB}{\mathcal V_B})\ge 0\]
    (12.5)

    In words: A unit push along the contact normal is the wrench ([p]n̂, n̂); the bodies may separate or slide but not penetrate.

    • ℱ contact wrench
    • p contact point
    • [·] bracket: skew-symmetric or se(3) matrix
    • n̂ unit contact normal
    • 𝒱A twist of body A
    • 𝒱B twist of body B
    Form closure test §12.1.7
    \[\text{contact wrenches }\class{sym-Fj}{\mathcal F_i}\text{ positively span }\class{sym-Rn}{\mathbb R}^3\ (\text{planar})\text{ or }\class{sym-Rn}{\mathbb R}^6\]

    In words: A part is in form closure when its contact wrenches can make every wrench by nonnegative combination.

    • ℱi wrench of contact i
    • ℝn real vector space

    Each contact is labeled rolling or sticking (R), sliding (S) or breaking (B). The same models predict pushing, carrying and whether a stack of blocks stands.

    Simplified: planar
