    Interactive

    Contact labels: B, R or S

    Ch 12 · §12.1.2§12.2.1Simplified: particle contact

    TrySet the angle to 0° and raise the push until the label turns S. Then lower μ and watch sliding start at a smaller push.
    Diagram

    How a contact gets its label

    Eq. 12.5Eq. 12.8

    The lit path is the label for the push above. The unit wrench F acts along the normal n̂ into body A. Rolling means ṗA = ṗB; otherwise the contact slides.

    How the demo decides (Sec. 12.3): the table is stationary, so 𝒱B = 0. The block starts at rest and only translates, so Fᵀ𝒱A = n̂ᵀvA. It tries each label and keeps the one where the contact force obeys ft ≤ μfn with fn ≥ 0, and the block's acceleration matches the label.

    The block is treated as a particle at one contact point: tipping is not modeled, and one friction coefficient μ is used, with no separate static and kinetic values. A penetrating motion is never feasible.

    Interactive

    Grasp builder: form and force closure

    Ch 12 · §12.1.7Eq. 12.14Simplified: planar, first order

    TryRemove contact 4 from the square: one shaded region appears. Then switch to Friction μ and find two contacts that give force closure.

    Each contact force n̂i at pi gives the planar wrench ℱi = (miz, fix, fiy) with miz = pixfiy − piyfix, measured in the fixed frame drawn at the center. The test is the book's (Sec. 12.1.7.2): rank F = 3, and the linear program (12.14) has a solution: find k minimizing 1Tk such that Fk = 0 and ki ≥ 1.

    With friction, each contact contributes the two friction-cone edges, and the same test gives force closure (Sec. 12.2.3). With μ = 0 force closure is first-order form closure. The analysis is first order: curvature effects (Fig. 12.14) are ignored.

    Part 4 · Ch 13 · Mobile robots

    13Driving: when you can't slide sideways

    A wheeled base moves in the plane with configuration q = (φ, x, y). Nonholonomic robots can't slide sideways, yet still reach every configuration.

    Ch 13 · §13.1–13.51 playgroundQuiz · 3 questions

    Orientation

    Why this exists

    A warehouse robot must drive to a shelf, park and reach for a box. Omniwheels let a base move in any direction; ordinary wheels can't slide sideways, so a car must maneuver. That no-slip rule limits velocities but not the configurations the robot can reach.

    After this you can
    • Convert between q̇ and the chassis twist 𝒱b = (ωbz, vbx, vby).
    • Compute wheel speeds from a desired twist for an omnidirectional base: u = H(0)𝒱b.
    • Write the canonical nonholonomic model q̇ = G(q)u and the diff-drive wheel equations.
    • Explain why a car can still reach any pose, and name its shortest-path families.
    • Estimate the chassis pose by odometry and control a mobile manipulator through one Jacobian.
    How it connects
    ← Builds onCh 2Configuration spaceCh 3Rigid-body motionsCh 5Jacobian and staticsCh 10Motion planningCh 11Robot control
    Leads to →Ch 4–11Robot playgroundApp AFormula sheet

    Key concepts

    Chassis configuration q

    The heading and position (φ, x, y) of the chassis frame {b} in the plane.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Omnidirectional robot

    A base with omniwheels or mecanum wheels that has no velocity equality constraint on its chassis.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Nonholonomic robot

    A base whose no-slip velocity constraint can't be integrated into a constraint on q.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Control vector fields

    The columns gᵢ(q) of G(q). Each is a direction of motion the controls can produce.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Lie bracket

    A new vector field [g₁, g₂] that shows a direction reachable by alternating motions along g₁ and g₂.

    See it in the lab ↗

    STLC

    Small-time locally controllable: the robot can maneuver locally in any direction in arbitrarily short time.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Odometry

    Pose estimation from how far the wheels have rotated, assuming no skidding or sideways slip.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Mobile manipulator Jacobian Je

    Maps wheel speeds u and joint rates θ̇ to the end-effector twist 𝒱e.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Where it happens

    The robot pipeline, from modeling to motion, with this chapter marked. Use the step buttons to walk through it.

    Worked example

    One odometry update for a diff-drive

    Ch 13 · §13.4
    §13.4Our choice: the numbers
    Odometry for a diff-drive Eq. 13.34–13.36
    𝒱b = FΔθ → Δqb → Δq → qk+1 = qk + Δq
    𝒱b = (0.5, 0.9, 0)
    Δqb = (0.500, 0.863, 0.220)
    Δq = (0.500, 0.637, 0.622)
    qk+1 = (1.024, 1.637, 1.122)

    In words: Wheel increments give the body twist 𝒱b = FΔθ; integrate it, rotate it into {s}, and add it to qk.

    • 𝒱b body twist of the chassis
    • F maps wheel increments to the twist
    • Δθ wheel angle increments
    • Δqb configuration change in {b}
    • Δq configuration change in {s}
    • qk+1 new chassis configuration
    • qk chassis configuration at step k

    Given. A diff-drive with r = 0.1 m, d = 0.2 m sits at qk = (30°, 1.0, 0.5). Encoders report ΔθL = 8 rad, ΔθR = 10 rad.

    Body twist. Eq. 13.34: ωbz = r(ΔθR − ΔθL)/(2d) = 0.5 rad, vbx = r(ΔθL + ΔθR)/2 = 0.9 m and vby = 0.

    Displacement in {b}. Since ωbz ≠ 0, Eq. 13.35 gives Δqb = (0.500, 0.863, 0.220): the chassis drives along an arc.

    Rotate into {s}. Eq. 13.36 rotates the position part by φk = 30°, giving Δq = (0.500, 0.637, 0.622).

    Result. qk+1 = qk + Δq = (1.024 rad ≈ 58.6°, 1.637, 1.122). The update repeats each time the encoders are read.

    The rule

    Hover a symbol to light it up in every equation and diagram of this chapter.

    No-slip (Pfaffian) constraint §13.3.1
    \[\class{sym-x13d}{\dot x}\sin\class{sym-phi13}{\phi}-\class{sym-y13d}{\dot y}\cos\class{sym-phi13}{\phi}=0\]

    In words: The wheels cannot slide sideways: the velocity perpendicular to the heading φ is zero.

    • ẋ chassis velocity along x̂
    • φ chassis heading angle
    • ẏ chassis velocity along ŷ
    Canonical nonholonomic model §13.3.1
    \[\begin{bmatrix}\class{sym-phi13d}{\dot{\phi}}\\\class{sym-x13d}{ \dot x}\\\class{sym-y13d}{ \dot y}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ \cos\class{sym-phi13}{\phi}&0\\ \sin\class{sym-phi13}{\phi}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\class{sym-v13}{v}\\\class{sym-w13}{ \omega}\end{bmatrix}\]
    (13.18)

    In words: The chassis can only drive forward at speed v and turn at rate ω.

    • φ̇ chassis turning rate
    • ẋ chassis velocity along x̂
    • ẏ chassis velocity along ŷ
    • φ chassis heading angle
    • v forward speed
    • ω turning rate of the chassis
    Diff-drive: wheel radius r, half-track d §13.3.1
    \[\class{sym-v13}{v}=\tfrac{\class{sym-rwheel}{r}}2(\class{sym-uL}{u_L}+\class{sym-uR}{u_R}),\qquad\class{sym-w13}{ \omega}=\tfrac{\class{sym-rwheel}{r}}{2\class{sym-dwheel}{d}}(\class{sym-uR}{u_R}-\class{sym-uL}{u_L})\]

    In words: Forward speed is r times the average wheel speed; the turning rate is r times their difference over 2d.

    • v forward speed
    • r wheel radius
    • uL left wheel speed
    • uR right wheel speed
    • ω turning rate of the chassis
    • d half the distance between wheels

    Mobile manipulation stacks base and arm into one Jacobian Je that maps wheel and joint rates to the end-effector twist.

    Mobile manipulation: base and arm share one Jacobian

    Ch 13 · §13.5Eq. 13.37Simplified: planarOur choice: weights, limits

    Wheel speeds u (rad/s)

    Joint rates θ̇ (rad/s)

    TryLock the base and watch the error grow once the target leaves the arm's reach. Then switch to Mecanum: the chassis can now slide sideways.
    RunningChanging the base or path restarts the run.
    Feedforward plus PI control through Je Eq. 13.37
    \[\begin{aligned}\class{sym-Vcmd}{\mathcal V}(\class{sym-t}{t})={}&[\class{sym-Ad}{\mathrm{Ad}}_{\class{sym-X13}{X}^{-1}\class{sym-Xd}{X_d}}]\class{sym-Vd}{\mathcal V_d}(\class{sym-t}{t})+\class{sym-Kp}{K_p}\class{sym-Xerr}{X_{\rm err}}(\class{sym-t}{t})\\&+\class{sym-Ki}{K_i}\!\int_0^\class{sym-t}{t}\!\class{sym-Xerr}{X_{\rm err}}(\class{sym-t}{t})\,dt\end{aligned}\]\[\begin{gathered}\begin{bmatrix}\class{sym-u}{u}\\\class{sym-thetad}{ \dot\theta}\end{bmatrix}=\class{sym-Jedag}{J_e^\dagger}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})\,\class{sym-Vcmd}{\mathcal V}\\[2pt]\class{sym-Je}{J_e}=\big[\,[\class{sym-Ad}{\mathrm{Ad}}_{\class{sym-T-0e}{T_{0e}}^{-1}\class{sym-T-b0}{T_{b0}}^{-1}}]\class{sym-F6}{F_6}\;\;\class{sym-Jarm}{J_{\rm arm}}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta})\big]\end{gathered}\]

    In words: The commanded twist is the desired twist, moved into the current end-effector frame, plus PI feedback on the configuration error.

    In words: The pseudoinverse of the combined base–arm Jacobian Je turns that twist into wheel speeds and joint rates.

    • 𝒱 commanded end-effector twist
    • t time
    • [AdT] adjoint representation of T
    • X end-effector configuration
    • Xd desired end-effector configuration
    • 𝒱d desired twist
    • Kp proportional gain
    • Xerr configuration error (as a twist)
    • Ki integral gain
    • u wheel driving speeds
    • θ̇ joint velocities
    • Je† pseudoinverse of Je
    • θ joint variables (angles or displacements)
    • Je Jacobian of base and arm together
    • T0e(θ) end-effector {e} in the arm base {0}
    • Tb0 arm base {0} in the chassis {b}
    • F6 F padded to six rows
    • Jarm body Jacobian of the arm

    The end-effector configuration is X = Tsb(q)Tb0T0e(θ). Wheel speeds u move the chassis through its F matrix, 𝒱b = Fu, and Jbase re-expresses that chassis twist in {e}. For the diff-drive, F has a row of zeros for vby: the chassis can't slide sideways, yet the arm lets the hand move sideways anyway.

    Here everything is planar, so twists and Xerr are 3-vectors (ω, vx, vy) and F6 reduces to F. The hand keeps a fixed heading, so the arm must turn against the chassis.

    As Section 13.5 allows, Je† is a weighted pseudoinverse: joint rates cost 100 times more than wheel speeds. The weight, the speed limits and the cap on ∫Xerr are our simulation choices, not from the book.

    ·One arm, every chapter at once

    A planar 3R arm with real dynamics. Drag the hand to explore the Jacobian, or run a task through IK, trajectory and control.

    Ch 4–111 playgroundNot in the book

    Orientation

    Why this exists

    Each chapter solves one piece of the problem, but a real robot needs them all at once. The playground runs inverse kinematics, time scaling, control and dynamics on one simulated arm, so you can see where each piece matters.

    After this you can
    • Trace a goal through IK, time scaling, control and dynamics, naming each chapter.
    • Use the null space of J to change a redundant arm's posture, hand fixed.
    • Relate the manipulability ellipse and gravity torques to the arm's posture.
    • Compare PD, PD + gravity and computed torque on the same task.
    • Judge how much computed torque depends on an accurate mass model.
    How it connects
    ← Builds onCh 4Forward kinematicsCh 5Jacobian and staticsCh 6Inverse kinematicsCh 8DynamicsCh 9Trajectory generationCh 11Robot control
    Leads to →Ch 10Motion planningCh 13Wheeled mobile robotsApp AFormula sheet

    Key concepts

    Pipeline

    The chain goal → IK → trajectory → controller → robot → sensors that turns a task into motion.

    Redundancy

    More joints than the task needs, which leaves a family of joint solutions for one hand position.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Null space of J

    Joint velocities that produce zero hand velocity.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Manipulability ellipse

    The image of unit joint speeds under J. It flattens to a line at a singularity.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Time scaling s(t)

    A function from 0 to 1 that sets how fast the robot moves along a path.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Bandwidth ωₙ

    The natural frequency of the error dynamics. Higher ωₙ corrects errors faster but needs larger torques.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Model error

    The difference between the controller's M̃, h̃ and the true dynamics. Feedback must correct what it leaves.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Tracking error θd − θ

    How far each joint lags or leads the planned trajectory. The plot in task mode shows it over time.

    See it in the lab ↗

    Check yourself

    What changed?

    Three questions on what one method changed about the method before it.

    1.What does the pseudoinverse step change about Newton–Raphson IK?

    The pseudoinverse J† (§6.2) gives a step even when J is not square or is singular, where J⁻¹ does not exist.

    2.What does A* search add to Dijkstra’s search on a grid?

    A* ranks nodes by past cost plus an optimistic estimate of the cost to go (§10.2.4), so it expands fewer nodes.

    3.PID control grows from PD control. What does it add?

    With the integral term the joint can hold a nonzero torque at zero position error, so the steady-state error under gravity goes to zero (§11.4.1).

    Check yourself

    Tell them apart

    Three questions on how methods of one family differ, from the methods tables.

    1.Which IK method needs no initial guess?

    Analytic IK finds both solutions in closed form (§6.1). The Newton–Raphson methods iterate from a guess θ⁰ and find the solution nearest it (§6.2).

    2.Which planner is probabilistically complete rather than resolution complete?

    Grid searches are resolution complete (§10.4). RRT grows a tree toward random samples and is probabilistically complete (§10.5).

    3.Impedance and admittance control both render a mass, spring and damper. Which one senses the external force and commands motion?

    Admittance control senses fext with a wrist force–torque sensor and responds with motion (§11.7.2); impedance control uses the model instead (§11.7.1).

    \[\begin{gathered}{}\class{sym-brk}{[}\class{sym-Vb}{\mathcal V_b}\class{sym-brk}{]}=\class{sym-logm}{\log}\!\big(\class{sym-T-sb}{T_{sb}}^{-1}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta}^i)\class{sym-T-sd}{T_{sd}}\big)\\[2pt]\class{sym-theta}{\theta}^{i+1}=\class{sym-theta}{\theta}^i+\class{sym-Jbdag}{J_b^{\dagger}}(\class{sym-theta}{\theta}^i)\,\class{sym-Vb}{\mathcal V_b}\end{gathered}\]

    • q chassis configuration (φ, x, y)

    Approximate motion along [g1, g2] comes from switching between g1 and g2. It is slow, like a car parallel parking.

    Terms on one robot

    A mobile manipulator uses nearly every idea in the book at once. Pick a term to open its card and light up its part. Pick a part to list its terms.

    No map terms match

    Clear the search or pick another category. The full list may still have it.

    How the pieces fit. A planner finds a path past the obstacle, and a time scaling turns it into a trajectory. The controller turns that trajectory into motor torques using the dynamics model and feedback from the encoders and the wrist force–torque sensor.

    Kinematics ties the joint values to the gripper frame {b} in {s}, and contact mechanics decides whether the object stays in the grasp. The map shows 81 of the 193 terms; the list has them all. Definitions follow the book's wording and notation; section numbers point to Modern Robotics (2019 preprint).
